claims.claim: Kullmann inverts Lubbock/Friedman: the omniscient archaic passages are the vivid visual 'showing', while point-of-view passages mainly serve to show states of mind rather than to describe action (p. 120).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: mainly serve to show certain states of mind

claims.claim: Kullmann notes the shift from Genette's focalisation externe to focalisation interne on Frodo, who becomes Bal's 'focalisé' or Lanser's 'focalizer', but he prefers the historical term 'point of view' (p. 123).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside

claims.feature: hobbit viewpoint vs archaic speech registers
claims.claim: The archaic register of Dwarves and Men contrasts starkly with the language of the hobbits and of the narrator, who usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view (p. 217).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: usually tells the story from the hobbits' points of view

claims.claim: Turner: Kullmann's psychonarration, events filtered through an individual's limited point of view, is typical of the realistic novel; where no hobbits are present the focus on 'archaic' characters brings narrative language of an older epic tradition.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)

claims.claim: Turner: K&S dispel any notion of one 'Tolkien style', showing skilful use of several styles resonating with the last few hundred years of English writing.
claims.source: Allan Turner, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Inklings Studies 12.1 (2022)
claims.quote: dispel any notion that there is any one ‘Tolkien style’

claims.feature: parataxis vs hypotaxis as cultural registers
claims.claim: Bolding reports Kullmann's contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis as defining the Rohirrim and Gondor cultures, with Gandalf the one speaker who moves fluidly between social registers.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: his contrast of parataxis and hypotaxis

claims.claim: Bolding summarises ch. 9: Gandalf and Frodo are the most flexible speakers, Sam undergoes the most evolution, Gimli and Legolas keep the most traditional registers, Merry and Pippin use common English as reality-based touchstones.
claims.source: Sharon L. Bolding, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Mythlore 41.1 (2022)
claims.quote: Gandalf and Frodo are found to be the most flexible

claims.claim: Holmes cites K&S data that Aragorn opens future pronouncements with 'shall' half again as often as Gandalf and seven times as often as Sam or Pippin.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: seven times as often as Sam or Pippin

claims.claim: Holmes: K&S's data tend to refute the long-held view of the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions in Tolkien (K&S p. 40).
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: the prevalence and significance of archaic inversions

claims.claim: Holmes: Kullmann identifies 45 to 50 intercalated stories told by twenty-three characters, in three categories (simultaneous events, exposition, mythological past); Bolding gives 23 storytellers.
claims.source: John R. Holmes, review of Kullmann & Siepmann, Journal of Tolkien Research 14.1 (2022)
claims.quote: 45 to 50 “intercalated” stories told by twenty-three characters

claims.claim: Siepmann's syntax chapter uses a corpus separating dialogue from narrative, with the PHRASEOROM post-war fiction corpus and the BNC as references, extracting the most significant 3- to 6-grams of syntactic tags and attending to constructions Tolkien avoids as well as prefers.
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, 'The Narrative Syntax of The Lord of the Rings' (ch. 3) abstract, Springer
claims.quote: constructions that Tolkien, compared to other authors, tends to avoid

claims.claim: Siepmann finds that the short copular sentences and modal 'would' uses that signal free indirect speech in modern fiction are conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings (pp. 75-76).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: conspicuous by their absence from The Lord of the Rings

claims.feature: inner monologue rendered by omniscient narrator
claims.claim: Short sentences of the kind found in modern fiction tend to be direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue, a strategy Tolkien does not use (p. 75).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: direct renditions by an omniscient narrator of characters' inner monologue

claims.claim: Instead of free indirect thought Tolkien overuses clauses reporting a character's thoughts with a that-clause ('He thought that he had heard a faint voice') and 'It seemed that' constructions (p. 84).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: It seemed that he had made some decision

claims.claim: At clause level the first thing to note is an evident underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position, against the contemporary-fiction patterns 'She longed to say it', 'He had expected to fight' (p. 74).
claims.source: Kullmann & Siepmann, Tolkien as a Literary Artist (2021), Google Books search-inside
claims.quote: underuse of personal pronouns in sentence-initial position
